pos: n. (inability to pay all one’s debts)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines insolvency as “Inability of a person to pay all his debts; or the state of wanting property sufficient for such payment.” Of an estate it is “Insufficiency to discharge all debts of the owner.” Scripture records insolvency’s weight on a household. A prophet’s widow cried that “the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen” (2Ki 4:1), and Elisha’s answer was to pay: “Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest” (2Ki 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INSOLVENCY, inability of a person to pay all his debts; insufficiency of an estate to discharge all debts of the owner.
webster_full: INSOLV'ENCY, noun [infra.] Inability of a person to pay all his debts; or the state of wanting property sufficient for such payment; as a merchant's insolvency
1. Insufficiency to discharge all debts of the owner; as the insolvency of an estate.
scriptures: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets unto Elisha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead; and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the LORD: and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen.
Then she came and told the man of God. And he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest.
Pro 22:7
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt.
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
corruption_summary: Insolvency is a debtor’s bondage; Scripture commands honest payment and shows mercy to the debtor who cannot pay.
corruption_paragraphs: “The borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). The insolvent man has lost the freedom his debts mortgaged.
“The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again” (Psa 37:21). The king of the parable “loosed him, and forgave him the debt” (Mat 18:27).
roots_summary: In- (not) and solvent: not able to pay.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): inability of a person to pay all his debts.
The borrower is servant to the lender (Pro 22:7).
usage: A merchant’s insolvency
The insolvency of an estate

pos: n. (uncoined gold or silver in the mass)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines bullion as “Uncoined gold or silver in the mass.” He adds that the precious metals are called bullion “when refined, but in bars, ingots, or in any form uncoined, as in plate.” Scripture weighs gold and silver in the mass: “Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold” (Gen 13:2), and David laid up “an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver” for the house of the LORD (1Ch 22:14). Wisdom outweighs it all: “My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold” (Pro 8:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BULLION, uncoined gold or silver in the mass, in bars, ingots or plate.
webster_full: BULL'ION, noun Uncoined gold or silver in the mass. The precious metals are called bullion when smelted and not perfectly refined, or when refined, but in bars, ingots, or in any form uncoined, as in plate.
scriptures: Gen 13:2
And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold.

Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the house of the LORD an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight; for it is in abundance: timber also and stone have I prepared; and thou mayest add thereto.
Job 28:1
Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it.
Pro 8:19
My fruit is better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver.
It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.
corruption_summary: Bullion is wealth in its plainest form; Scripture still ranks wisdom above it.
corruption_paragraphs: Job knew where metal comes from: “Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it” (Job 28:1).
Wisdom “cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof” (Job 28:15).
roots_summary: Uncoined gold or silver in the mass.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): uncoined gold or silver in the mass.
Neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof (Job 28:15).
usage: Uncoined gold or silver
In bars, ingots, or in any form uncoined

pos: n. (a share of profit; a number to be divided)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a dividend as “A part or share; particularly, the share of the interest or profit of stock in trade or other employment, which belongs to each proprietor according to his proportion of the stock or capital.” In arithmetic it is “the number to be divided into equal parts.” Joseph’s law in Egypt set a fixed share of the increase: “ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own” (Gen 47:24). In the parable each servant answered for the return on what he was given: “Occupy till I come” (Luk 19:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DIVIDEND, a part or share; the share of the profit of stock in trade belonging to each proprietor; in arithmetic, the number to be divided.
webster_full: DIVIDEND, noun
1. A part or share; particularly, the share of the interest or profit of stock in trade or other employment, which belongs to each proprietor according to his proportion of the stock or capital.
2. In arithmetic, the number to be divided into equal parts.
scriptures: And it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.
And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
Ecc 11:2
Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.
corruption_summary: A dividend is the owner’s share of increase; Scripture reminds every owner that the increase comes from God.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s dividend is paid “according to his proportion of the stock or capital.” The share follows the stake.
The Preacher counsels spreading the stake: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecc 11:2).
roots_summary: Latin dividendum: that which is to be divided.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a part or share.
Webster: the number to be divided into equal parts.
Occupy till I come (Luk 19:13).
usage: The share of the interest or profit of stock
The number to be divided

pos: n. (a mechanic hired to work for another)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a journeyman as “Strictly, a man hired to work by the day, but in fact, any mechanic who is hired to work for another in his employment, whether by the month, year or other term.” The word “is applied only to mechanics in their own occupations.” Paul worked as a hired craftsman with Aquila: “because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). The law protected the day-labourer’s pay: “the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning” (Lev 19:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JOURNEYMAN, strictly a man hired to work by the day; any mechanic hired to work for another in his occupation.
webster_full: JOUR'NEYMAN, noun

Strictly, a man hired to work by the day, but in fact, any mechanic who is hired to work for another in his employment, whether by the month, year or other term. It is applied only to mechanics in their own occupations.
scriptures: Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning.
At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee.
Mat 20:2
And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
corruption_summary: The journeyman sells his skill by the day; Scripture binds his master to pay him on time.
corruption_paragraphs: “At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it” (Deu 24:15).
The householder of the parable “agreed with the labourers for a penny a day” (Mat 20:2) and kept his word.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): strictly, a man hired to work by the day.
For by their occupation they were tentmakers (Act 18:3).
usage: Any mechanic who is hired to work for another
Hired to work by the day

pos: n. & v. (an officer of order; to arrange in order)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a marshal as “One who regulates rank and order at a feast or any other assembly, directs the order of procession and the like”, and “A harbinger; a pursuivant; one who goes before a prince to declare his coming.” In America he is “a civil officer, appointed by the President and Senate of the United States, in each judicial district, answering to the sheriff of a county.” The verb means “To dispose in order; to arrange in a suitable manner; as, to marshal an army.” Israel was marshalled in its camp: “Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard” (Num 2:2). John the Baptist went before the King as His harbinger: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight” (Mat 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MARSHAL, the chief officer of arms; one who regulates rank and order; a harbinger; in America a federal civil officer answering to a sheriff; v. to dispose in order.
webster_full: M'ARSHAL, noun
1. The chief officer of arms, whose duty it is to regulate combats in the lists.
2. One who regulates rank and order at a feast or any other assembly, directs the order of procession and the like.
3. A harbinger; a pursuivant; one who goes before a prince to declare his coming and provide entertainment.
4. In France, the highest military officer. In other countries of Europe, a marshal is a military officer of high rank, and called field-marshal.

5. In America, a civil officer, appointed by the President and Senate of the United States, in each judicial district, answering to the sheriff of a county. His duty is to execute all precepts directed to him, issued under the authority of the United States.
6. An officer of any private society, appointed to regulate their ceremonies and execute their orders.

Earl marshal of England, the eighth officer of state; an honorary title, and personal, until made hereditary by Charles II, in the family of Howard. During a vacancy in the office of high constable, the earl marshal has jurisdiction in the court of chivalry.
Earl marshal of Scotland. This officer formerly had command of the cavalry, under the constable. This office was held by the family of Keith, but forfeited by rebellion in 1715.

Knight marshal or marshal of the king's house, formerly an officer who was to execute the commands of the lord steward, and have the custody of prisoners committed by the court of verge; hence, the name of a prison in Southwark.
Marshal of the king's bench, an officer who has the custody of the prison called the king's bench, in Southwark. He attends on the court and has the charge of the prisoners committed by them.
MA'RSHAL, verb transitive To dispose in order; to arrange in a suitable manner; as, to marshal an army; to marshal troops.
1. To lead, as a harbinger. [Not used.]
2. To dispose in due order the several parts of an escutcheon, or the coats of arms of distinct families.
scriptures: Num 2:2
Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch.
Mat 3:3
For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Est 6:11

Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.
corruption_summary: A marshal keeps order and announces the king; the church’s order and John’s office both serve the King who comes.
corruption_paragraphs: At the king’s order Haman led Mordecai through the city and “proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour” (Est 6:11).
In worship: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
roots_summary: The officer of order, then the herald who goes before a prince.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): one who regulates rank and order at a feast or any other assembly.
Webster: to dispose in order.
Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard (Num 2:2).
usage: To marshal an army
Field-marshal

pos: n. (a meeting; an assembly of delegates; an agreement)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a convention as “The act of coming together; a meeting of several persons or individuals”, and as “an assembly of delegates or representatives for consultation on important concerns, civil, political or ecclesiastical.” In America it is “the assembly of representatives which forms a constitution of government, or political association; as the convention which formed the constitution of the United States in 1787.” It is also “An agreement or contract between two parties.” Israel’s leaders convened to hear a grave question before acting: when Phinehas and the princes “heard the words” of the eastern tribes, “it pleased them” (Jos 22:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONVENTION, a coming together; an assembly of delegates for consultation, as that which formed the constitution of the United States in 1787; an agreement between two parties.
webster_full: CONVENTION, noun [Latin See Convene.]
1. The act of coming together; a meeting of several persons or individuals.
2. Union; coalition.

3. An assembly. In this sense, the word includes any formal meeting or collection of men for civil or ecclesiastical purposes; particularly an assembly of delegates or representatives for consultation on important concerns, civil, political or ecclesiastical. In Great Britain, convention is the name given to an extraordinary assembly of the estates of the realm, held without the kings writ; as the assembly which restored Charles II. to the throne, and that which declared the throne to be abdicated by James II. In the United States, this name is given to the assembly of representatives which forms a constitution of government, or political association; as the convention which formed the constitution of the United States in 1787.
4. An agreement or contract between two parties, as between the commanders of two armies; an agreement previous to a definitive treaty.
scriptures: And when Phinehas the priest, and the princes of the congregation and heads of the thousands of Israel which were with him, heard the words that the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the children of Manasseh spake, it pleased them.
Act 15:6

Deu 1:15

So I took the chief of your tribes, wise men, and known, and made them heads over you, captains over thousands, and captains over hundreds, and captains over fifties, and captains over tens, and officers among your tribes.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
corruption_summary: A convention gathers delegates to deliberate; Scripture asks that they hear the matter fully before they judge.
corruption_paragraphs: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).
The council at Jerusalem met because “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the act of coming together.
Webster: an assembly of delegates or representatives.
The apostles and elders came together (Act 15:6).
usage: The convention which formed the constitution

pos: n. & adj. (one who acts in another’s place)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a representative as “an agent, deputy or substitute who supplies the place of another or others, being invested with his or their authority.” He gives examples: “An attorney is the representative of his client or employer.” In law it is “one that stands in the place of another as heir.” Scripture’s high priest bore the people before God: “Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart” (Exo 28:29). Christ is the one Representative of His people: “now to appear in the presence of God for us” (Heb 9:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REPRESENTATIVE, one that exhibits the likeness of another; an agent, deputy or substitute invested with another’s authority; in law, one who stands in another’s place as heir.
webster_full: REPRESENT'ATIVE, adjective
1. Exhibiting a similitude.
They own the legal sacrifices, though representative to be proper and real.
2. Bearing the character or power of another; as a council representative of the people.
REPRESENT'ATIVE, noun
1. One that exhibits the likeness of another.
A statue of Rumor, whispering an idiot in the ear, who was the representative of credulity.

2. In legislative or other business, an agent, deputy or substitute who supplies the place of another or others, being invested with his or their authority. An attorney is the representative of his client or employer. A member of the house of commons is the representative of his constituents and of the nation. In matters concerning his constituents only, he is supposed to be bound by their instructions, but in the enacting of laws for the nation, he is supposed not to be bound by their instructions, as he acts for the whole nation.
3. In law, one that stands in the place of another as heir, or in the right of succeeding to an estate of inheritance, or to a crown.
4. That by which any thing is exhibited or shown.
This doctrine supposes the perfections of God to be the representatives to us of whatever we perceive in the creatures.
scriptures: And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually.
Heb 9:24
For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us:

For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: Every man is represented by Adam or by Christ; civil representation is a lesser copy of that greater truth.
corruption_paragraphs: “For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19).
Believers become representatives in turn: “we are ambassadors for Christ” (2Co 5:20).
roots_summary: Re- and present: to present again, in another’s place.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): one that exhibits the likeness of another.
Webster: an agent, deputy or substitute who supplies the place of another.
To appear in the presence of God for us (Heb 9:24).
usage: A council representative of the people
The representative of his constituents

pos: n. (a succession of kings of the same line)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr. power, sovereignty; a lord or chief; to be able or strong, to prevail.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a dynasty as “Government; sovereignty; or rather a race or succession of kings of the same line or family, who govern a particular country.” He adds, “The obligation of treaties and contracts is allowed to survive the change of dynasties.” God promised David a dynasty: “thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever” (2Sa 7:16). The angel announced its Heir: “the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David” (Luk 1:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DYNASTY, government; sovereignty; a race or succession of kings of the same line or family.
webster_full: DY'NASTY, noun [Gr. power, sovereignty; a lord or chief; to be able or strong, to prevail.]
Government; sovereignty; or rather a race or succession of kings of the same line or family, who govern a particular country;

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines commerce as “an interchange or mutual change of goods, wares, productions, or property of any kind, between nations or individuals, either by barter, or by purchase and sale; trade; traffick.” It also means “Intercourse between individuals; interchange of work, business, civilities or amusements; mutual dealings in common life.” The virtuous wife trades: “She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant” (Pro 31:24). Tyre’s commerce made her proud: “By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches” (Eze 28:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): COMMERCE, an interchange of goods between nations or individuals, by barter or purchase and sale; trade; intercourse; v. to traffick.
webster_full: COMMERCE, noun

1. In a general sense, an interchange or mutual change of goods, wares, productions, or property of any kind, between nations or individuals, either by barter, or by purchase and sale; trade; traffick. commerce is foreign or inland. Foreign commerce is the trade which one nation carries on with another; inland commerce or inland trade, is the trade in the exchange of commodities between citizens of the same nation or state. Active commerce
2. Intercourse between individuals; interchange of work, business, civilities or amusements; mutual dealings in common life.
3. Familiar intercourse between the sexes.
4. Interchange; reciprocal communications; as, there is a vast commerce of ideas.
COMMERCE, verb intransitive
1. To traffick; to carry on trade.
2. To hold intercourse with.
And looks commercing with the skies.

corruption_paragraphs: James rebukes merchants who plan to “buy and sell, and get gain” with no thought of God (Jas 4:13).
When Babylon falls, “the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her” (Rev 18:11).
roots_lines: Webster (1828): an interchange or mutual change of goods.
Webster: mutual dealings in common life.
She maketh fine linen, and selleth it (Pro 31:24).

pos: n. (a plea that the facts, if true, do not support the claim)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a demurrer in law as “a stop at some point in the pleadings, and a resting of the decision of the cause on that point; an issue on matter of law.” He explains: “A demurrer confesses the fact or facts to be true, but denies the sufficiency of the facts in point of law to support the claim or defense.” Scripture names no such plea. It does show the courtroom reasoning of a man answering for himself, as when Paul “answered, Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself” (Act 24:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DEMURRER, in law, a stop in the pleadings resting the cause on a point of law; it confesses the facts but denies their sufficiency in law.
webster_full: DEMURRER, noun

2. In law, a stop at some point in the pleadings, and a resting of the decision of the cause on that point; an issue on matter of law. A demurrer confesses the fact or facts to be true, but denies the sufficiency of the facts in point of law to support the claim or defense. A demurrer may be tendered to the declaration, to the plea, to the replication, to the rejoinder, etc.
scriptures: Then Paul, after that the governor had beckoned unto him to speak, answered, Forasmuch as I know that thou hast been of many years a judge unto this nation, I do the more cheerfully answer for myself:
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
corruption_summary: A demurrer grants the facts and argues the law; before God no sinner can plead that his facts are insufficient.
corruption_paragraphs: The demurrer asks whether the facts, granted, make a case. Wise judges first hear the matter: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).
God opens His own court to reason with the guilty: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD” (Isa 1:18).
roots_summary: Demur, to stop: a stop in the pleadings.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): in law, a stop at some point in the pleadings.
Come now, and let us reason together (Isa 1:18).
usage: An issue on matter of law
A demurrer may be tendered to the declaration
